summary: Back by the Sea of Galilee in the Decapolis, Jesus heals crowds of sick people and, taking one deaf man aside, opens his ears and loosens his tongue.
key_insight: Mark’s word for “an impediment in his speech” appears nowhere else in the New Testament. In the Greek Old Testament it appears in Isaiah 35:6, where “the tongue of the dumb” will sing when God comes to save. The crowd’s cry, “He makes both the deaf to hear and the mute to speak,” is Isaiah’s promise coming true in Gentile country.
story: Jesus left the region of Tyre and Sidon and came back to the Sea of Galilee, passing through the region of the Decapolis. {Mk} He went up on a mountain and sat down there. {Mt}
Great crowds came to Him, bringing the lame, the blind, the mute, the maimed and many others. They laid them down at Jesus’ feet, and He healed them. {Mt}

Some people brought Him a man who was deaf and had an impediment in his speech, and they begged Jesus to put His hand on him. Jesus took him aside from the crowd, put His fingers in his ears, spat, and touched his tongue. Then, looking up to heaven, He sighed and said to him, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened.” {Mk}

Immediately his ears were opened, the impediment of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke plainly. Jesus commanded them to tell no one, but the more He commanded them, the more widely they proclaimed it. {Mk}

The people were astonished beyond measure. “He has done all things well,” they said. “He makes both the deaf to hear and the mute to speak.” {Mk} When the crowds saw the mute speaking, the maimed made whole, the lame walking and the blind seeing, they glorified the God of Israel. {Mt}
differences: Matthew describes many healings on a mountain; Mark describes one healing in detail.
Only Mark tells of the deaf man, the fingers in his ears, the spitting, the sigh and the Aramaic word “Ephphatha.”
Matthew says the crowds “glorified the God of Israel”; Mark records their words, “He has done all things well.”
Mark says Jesus came “through the midst of the region of Decapolis”; Matthew says He “skirted the Sea of Galilee.”

scene.label: A long way round
scene.text: From the coast near Tyre, Jesus did not take the short road home. He came back through the Decapolis, mostly Gentile country east of the lake, where the man freed from Legion had been telling what Jesus had done for him (Mark 5:20). Now people there bring their sick to Jesus.

scene.label: Fingers and spit
scene.text: People in the ancient world commonly believed saliva had healing power. Jesus used touch the deaf man could feel, and gestures he could see: ears, tongue, a look to heaven. He used spittle again with the blind man at Bethsaida (Mark 8:23) and the man born blind (John 9:6).

scene.label: “Ephphatha”
scene.text: Jesus spoke Aramaic, the everyday language of Galilee. Mark keeps the very word Jesus used, then translates it for his readers: “Be opened.”

scene.label: “The God of Israel”
scene.text: Matthew’s phrase suggests that many in this crowd were Gentiles. People who did not belong to Israel praised Israel’s God for what Jesus had done.

witnesses.matthew: Summarizes a wave of healings on a mountain, as he often does, and notes that the crowds “glorified the God of Israel,” probably Gentiles praising Israel’s God. The scene sets up the feeding of the four thousand, the same crowd after three days with Jesus (15:32).
witnesses.mark: Picks out one man and tells it slowly: taken aside, fingers in his ears, a touch on his tongue, a sigh, an Aramaic word. This healing and the blind man at Bethsaida (8:22–26) are the only two miracles found in Mark alone, and they frame his chapter about disciples who, “having ears,” do not hear (8:18).

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the One Isaiah promised, who makes the deaf hear and the mute speak, and He gives this gift in Gentile country. He deals with one man in a way he could understand, through touch and sight, before speaking the word that opened his ears.
seeing.living: Jesus took the man aside, away from the crowd, and dealt with him personally. He still meets people one at a time and in ways they can grasp. Ask Him to open your ears to His word, and then do not keep quiet about what He has done.
seeing.ponder: Where do you need Jesus to say “Be opened” in your life: your ears to His word, or your mouth to speak of Him?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus does all things well: He opens deaf ears and loosens silent tongues.
outline: A praise that would not be hushed (36–37)
preaching.watch_for: Watch the two commands. “Be opened” (v. 34) is obeyed at once; “tell no one” (v. 36) is not. The crowd’s closing verdict, “He has done all things well” (v. 37), may echo God’s verdict on creation, “it was very good” (Genesis 1:31).
